div.head: Real-time round robin, a novel real-time scheduling algorithm, is proposed in this paper. It is a time slot-based algorithm. Tasks are divided into groups and each group of tasks is statically assigned a subset of time slots. In a group, tasks are scheduled by earliest deadline first.
div.p: We introduce "regular" subsets of time slots. It has the advantage that any periodic tasks can be scheduled only at time slots contained in the subset using the minimum num- ber of time slots. We show a method to divide the universal set of time slots into at least two regular subsets.

Consequently, real-time round robin can schedule periodic tasks whose processor utilization factor does not exceeds 100% at less scheduling cost than that of earliest deadline first. Moreovel; no deadline miss of a task in one group affect tasks in any other groups.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Rate monotonic and earliest deadline first scheduling algorithm [3] [5] are two major real-time scheduling algorithms for periodic tasks. However, both algorithms have their shortcomings. Rate monotonic causes a deadline miss when the processor utilization factor is more than In 2 (69.3%) in the worst case (88% in the average case [2]).

Earliest deadline first scheduling algorithm can achieve the processor utilization factor of loo%, but it has the following three shortcomings. First, the scheduling cost of earliest deadline first is more than that of rate monotonic. Second, since tasks are not assigned fixed priorities, important tasks can cause a deadline miss which results from a transient overload of less important tasks. Third, delay caused by one task affects scheduling of successive tasks and may cause many deadline misses as a consequence. *Author's current address is C&C media research laboratories, NEC Corporation, 4-1-1 Miyazaki, Miyamae-ku, Kawasaki, Japan.

Cyclic executive is an algorithm which does not assign priority to tasks. The scheduling cost of this algorithm is 0(1), whereas the algorithms described above have a scheduling cost of O(1ogn) where n is the number of tasks. The most serious disadvantage of cyclic executive is "fragility" as pointed out in [4]. Fragility means that any change to the system will cause a deadline miss. For example, when a new task arrives, all tasks need to be rescheduled. It costs high to schedule all tasks without any simple schedulability condition.
In this paper, we propose a novel scheduling algorithm, real-time round robin. This algorithm overcomes the disadvantages of both earliest deadline first and cyclic executive.

Real-time round robin is a time slot-based scheduling algorithm for periodic tasks. Periodic tasks are divided into groups. Each group of tasks is statically assigned a disjoint subset of time slots in advance, and tasks in a group is assigned a processor on its subset of time slots. Each task group is statically scheduled on the time slots assigned to the task group.

Because of the isolation of groups of tasks and their static schedule, real-time round robin has the following advantages: 0 The scheduling cost can be reduced by partitioning tasks scheduled by earliest deadline first into small groups.

e A transient overload caused by a task in one group does not affect the scheduling of tasks in other groups. Due to the advantage, hard real-time tasks can be scheduled more safely when they are assigned more time slots, while soft real-time tasks can be assigned less time slots to relax the schedulability condition.

Tasks in a task group are scheduled only using the time slots assigned to the task group. The scheduling algorithm in a group of tasks under real-time round robin is earliest deadline first, which can fully utilize a processor when all time slots are available. However, even if task groups are assigned enough time slots to fulfill the computation time requirement, deadline misses may still occur by scheduling tasks using earliest deadline first on the subset of time slots.

For example, suppose that a periodic task whose period and computation time are 4 and 1 respectively is scheduled by earliest deadline first. In Figure 1, (a) and (b) shows two different assignment of time slots to the task. Both (a) and (b) contain four time slots out of eight. The rectangles represents time slots which belongs to (a) or (b). The gray rectangles represents a time slot used for the execution of the task, the white ones represents time slots assigned to the task but is not for execution. Both examples assign the same number of time slots to the task, but there are deadline misses on (a) because there is no time slot assigned between the time slot from 4 to 8 while there are four time slot between time slot from 0 to 3. It is caused by uneven distribution of time slots. The above example shows that a deadline miss is not caused only by the shortage of time slots in a subset, but also on which time slots a subset contains. We classify subsets of time slots according to the schedulability conditions on them. Subsets which can be fully utilized by execution of tasks, which is called "regular", are formulated in this paper.

We classify all subsets of time slots in Section 2 and show the schedulability conditions on all classes in Section 3. Scheduling algorithm of real-time round robin is discussed in Section 4. div.head: Real-time round robin
div.p: Regular time slot sets are assigned to all task groups to fully utilize a processor. First, we show how to calculate the location of time slots constituting regular time slot sets. Then, we describe how to combine multiple regular time slot sets to schedule multiple task groups. Finally we explain the algorithm of real-time round robin.

div.p: The algorithm of real-time round robin is as follows. We assume that all task groups require only regular time slot sets which are made by Theorem 4.2 and 4.3. Time slot sets are made and assigned to task groups both statically and dynamically.

This step is performed at runtime. Division of a general task set into more than two groups is not considered in this paper. Under this restriction on a task set, real-time round robin can schedule a general task set whose demand factor is less than or equal to 1.

Arrival of a task whose demand factor is more than the available capacity of any regular time slot set, but less than the sum of all available capacities, cause re-division of time slot sets to make enough capacity. Hence, if the number of task groups are less than three, a new task can be scheduled as long as the demand factor of a task set is less than or equal to 1. The cost of the division depends on the number of tasks. When a task terminates, no re-scheduling is required. Figure 5 shows an example. A task set which includes four task groups whose demand factors are 4/11, 3/11, 2/11 and 2/11 is scheduled. The algorithm can be easily expanded into the algorithm on multiprocessor system by application of real-time round robin to each processor.

If the size is P , the denominator of the densities of time slot sets must be a divisor of P . A timetable whose size is P can be represented by less size of a timetable when it is made by division of regular time slot set. So, the size needed is the maximum interval of time slots in regular time slots.

div.head: Related works
div.p: We compare real-time round robin and existing algorithms in this section. The proportional share resource allocation algorithm [7] assign a processor to tasks for the time in proportion to their weight at each unit of time. However, the algorithm requires context switches among tasks within each time slot The number of context switches required under real-time round robin is less than that of proportional share resource. Two-level hierarchical scheme [ 11 also divides taskshto task groups. Each subset of tasks has its own scheduler, and the task groups are scheduled by the total bandwidth server [6]. The scheduling of task groups makes overhead. Real-time round robin schedules task groups statically to reduce the overhead.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We show a new real-time scheduling algorithm, realtime round robin in this paper. We classify all subsets of time slots according to their schedulability condition. By statically scheduling isolated groups of tasks, we overcome three problems of earliest deadline first. First, a transient overload in a task group never affects tasks in the other task groups because of the isolation. Second, the scheduling cost is reduced because the number of tasks to be scheduled is reduced by the static schedule. Third, importance of a task group can be taken into consideration because important task groups can be assigned a processor more than needed to prevent transient overloads from causing a deadline miss and unimportant task groups can be assigned a processor less than needed to execute more tasks with deadline misses in the groups. In addition, unlike cyclic executives, the algorithm can accept new tasks without always re-scheduling a task set because of the schedulability conditions.

We show that subsets of time slots called regular can be fully utilized, and that two arbitrary regular subsets can be generated. The algorithm can fully utilize a processor when there are less than three groups of tasks. Moreover, regular subsets can be divided evenly into regular ones. An arbitrary task set is divided into more than two task groups in special cases. Work is in progress to extend our algorithm to handle the general case with more than two task groups.
